source_text: Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberii proponit eum descendisse in ciuitatem Galilaeae Capharnaum, utique de caelo creatoris, in quod de suo ante descenderat. ecquid ergo ordinis fuerat, ut prius de suo caelo in creatoris descendens describeretur? cur enim non et ista reprehendam, quae non implent fidem ordinariae narrationis, deficientis in mendacio semper? plane semel dicta sint per quae iam alibi retractauimus: an descendens per creatorem, et quidem aduersus ipsum, potuerit ab eo admitti et inde tramitti in terram aeque ipsius. nunc autem et reliquum ordinem descensionis expostulo, tenens (descendisse) illum. uiderit enim, sicubi 'apparuisse* positum est. apparere subitum ex inopinato sapit conspectum, qui semel impegerit oculos in id, quod sine mora apparuit, descendisse autem dum fit uidetur et subicit oculos de facto. etiam ordinem facit atque ita cogit exigere, quali habitu, quali suggestu, quonam impetu uel temperamento, etiam quo in tempore diei noctisue descenderit; praeterea, quis uiderit descendentem, quis retulerit, quis adseuerauerit rem, utique nec adseueranti facile credendam. indignum denique, ut Romulus quidem ascensus sui in caelum habuerit Proculum adfirmatorem, Christus uero dei descensus de caelo sui non inuenerit adnuntiatorem, *** quasi non sic et ille ascenderit isdem mendacii scalis, sicut et iste descendit. quid autem illi cum Galilaea. si non erat creatoris, cui ista regio destinabatur ingressuro praedicationem, dicente Esaia: hoc primum bibito, cito facito, regio Zabulon et terra Nepthalim, et ceteri quimaritimam, etIordanis, Galilaea nationum. populus, qui sedetis in tenebris, uidete lumen magnum; qui habitatis terram, sedentes in umbra mortis, lumen ortum est super uos? bene autem, quod et deus Marcionis inluminator uindicatur nationum, quo magis debuerit, uel de caelo etsi descenderet, utique in Pontum potius descendere quam in Galilaeam. ceterum et loco et inluminationis opere secundum praedicationem occurrentibus Christo iam eum prophetatum incipimus agnoscere, ostendentem in primo ingressu uenisse se, non ut legem et prophetas dissolueret, sed ut potius adimpleret. hoc enim Marcion ut additum erasit. sed frustra negabit Christum dixisse quod statim fecit ex parte. prophetiam enim interim de loco adimpleuit: de caelo statim. ad synagogam. ut dici solet: 'ad quod uenimus, hoc age Marcion: aufer etiam illud de euangelio: non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israhel, et: non est auferre panem filiis et dare eum canibus, ne scilicet Christus Israhelis uideatur. sufficiunt mihi facta pro dictis. detrahe uoces Christi mei: res loquentur. ecce uenit in synagogam: certe ad oues perditas domus Israhelis. ecce doctrinae suae panem prioribus offert Israhelitis: certe, ut filios praefert. ecce aliis eum nondum impertit: certe, ut canes praeterit. quibus autem magis impertisset quam extraneis creatoris, si ipse inprimis non fuisset creatoris? et tamen quomodo in synagogam potuit admitti tam repentinus, tam ignotus, cuius nemo adhuc certus de tribu, de populo, de domo, de censu denique Augusti, quem testem fidelissimum dominicae natiuitatis Romana archiua custodiunt? Meminerant certe, nisi circumcisum scirent, non admittendum in sancta sanctorum. sed etsi passim synagoga adiretur, non tamen ad docendum nisi ab optime cognito et explorato et probato iam pridem in hoc ipsum uel aliunde commendato cum hoc munere. stupebant autem omnes ad doctrinam eius. plane. quoniam, inquit, in potestate erat sermo eius, non quoniam aduersus legem et prophetas docebat. utique enim eloquium diuinum et uim et gratiam praestabat, magis exstruens quam destruens substantiam legis et prophetarum. alioquin non stuperent, sed horrerent, nec mirarentur, sed statim auersarentur destructorem legis et prophetarum, et utique inprimis alterius dei praedi. catorem, quia nec potuisset aduersus legem et prophetas docere et hoc nomine aduersus creatorem non praemissa diuersae atque aemulae diuinitatis professione. cum ergo nihil tale scriptura significet, nisi solam uim et potestatem sermonis admirationi fuisse, facilius ostendit secundum creatorem docuisse illum, quia non negauit, quam aduersus creatorem, quia non significauit. atque ita aut eius erit agnoscendus, secundum quem docuit, aut praeuaricator iudicandus, si secundum eum, aduersus quem uenerat, docuit. exclamat ibidem spiritus daemonis: quid nobis et tibi est, Iesu uenisti perdere nos; scio qui sis, sanctus dei. hic ego non retractabo, an et hoc cognomentum competierit ei, quem nec Christum uocari oporteret, si non creatoris, — alibi iam de nominibus expostulatum est — at nunc discepto, quomodo hoc eum uocari cognouerit daemon, nulla umquam retro emissa praedicatione in illum a deo ignoto et in id temporis muto, cuius nec sanctum eum contestari potuit, ut ignoti (et)iam ipsi suo creatori. quid autem iam tale ediderat nouae diuinitatis. per quod posset alterius dei sanctus intellegi? tantum quod synagogam introgressus et nec sermone operatus (erat) aliquid aduersus creatorem? sicut ergo quem ignorabat nullo modo poterat Iesum et sanctum dei agnoscere, ita quem norat agnouit. nam et prophetam meminerat sanctum dei praedicasse et Iesum nomen domini esse in filio Naue. haec et ab angelo exceperat secundum nostrum euangelium: propterea quod in te nascetur uocabitur sanctum, filius dei, et uocabis nomen eius Iesum. sed et habebat utique sensum aliquem dominicae dispositionis — licet daemon tamen — magis quam alienae et nondum satis cognitae. nam et praemisit: quid nobis et tibi, Iesu? non quasi in extraneum, (sed) ad quem pertinent spiritus creatoris. nec enim dixit: 'quid tibi et nobis'? sed 'quid nobis et tibi'? se deplorans et sorti suae exprobrans. quam iam uidens adicit: uenisti perdere nos. adeo iudicis et ultoris et, ut ita dixerim, saeui dei filium agnouerat Iesum, non optimi illius, et perdere et punire nescientis. quorsum hunc locum praemisimus? ut Iesum et a daemone non alium doceamus agnitum et a semetipso non alium confirmatum quam creatoris. 'atquin', inquis, 'increpuit illum Iesus). plane, ut inuidiosum et in ipsa confessione petulantem, ut male adulantem, quasi haec esset summa gloria Christi, si ad perditionem daemonum uenisset et non potius ad hominum salutem, qui nec discipulos de subactione spirituum, sed de candida salutis gloriari uolebat. aut cur eum increpuit? si quasi mentitum in totum, ergo non fuit Iesus nec dei sanctus omnino; si quasi ex parte mentitum, quod eum legum quidem et sanctum dei, sed creatoris, existimasset, iniustissime increpuit hoc sentientem, quod sciebat sentiendum, et hoc non aestimantem, quod ignorabat aestimandum: alium legum et alterius dei sanctum. quodsi uerisimiliorem statum non habet increpatio nisi quem nos interpretamur, iam ergo et daemon nihil mentitus est, non ob mendacium increpitus; ipse enim erat Iesus, praeter quem alium daemon agnouisse non poterat, et Iesus eum confirmauit, quem agnouerat daemon, dum non ob mendacium increpat daemonem.
pass_a_gloss: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, he proposes that he descended into the city of Galilee, Capharnaum, indeed from the heaven of the creator, into which he had previously descended from his own heaven. What order was there, therefore, that he should be described as having first descended from his own heaven into the heaven of the creator? Why should I not also reprehend these things, which do not fulfill the faith of the ordinary narrative, always failing in falsehood? Let what was once said be enough, through which we have already elsewhere retracted: whether, descending through the creator, and indeed against him, he could have been admitted by him and sent from there into the earth, equally his own. Now, however, I also demand the rest of the order of the descent, holding that he descended. For he sees, indeed, where it is written that he appeared. To appear suddenly, from the unexpected, has the flavor of a sudden sight, which, once it has struck the eyes on that which appeared without delay, seems to have descended, and it subjects the eyes to the fact. And it also makes an order and thus compels one to demand, with what habit, with what suggestion, with what impetus or temperament, and also at what time of day or night he descended; furthermore, who saw him descending, who reported it, who confirmed the thing, which is not easily to be believed even by one confirming it. It is finally unworthy that Romulus, indeed, had Proculus as a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Christ did not find an announcer of his descent from heaven, as if he did not also ascend by the same ladders of falsehood. What, therefore, does he have to do with Galilee? If it was not the creator's, to whom this region was destined for the entrance of preaching, saying, as Isaiah says: 'This first, drink quickly, the region of Zabulon and the land of Nepthalim, and the others who are by the sea, and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. A people who sit in darkness, see a great light; who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you?' It is good, indeed, that the god of Marcion is also vindicated as the illuminator of the nations, by which he ought all the more to have descended, even from heaven, into Pontus rather than into Galilee. Nevertheless, both in the place and in the work of illumination, according to the preaching, we begin to recognize Christ, who, in his first entrance, showed that he came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them. For Marcion erased this, which was added. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he immediately did in part. For he fulfilled the prophecy, meanwhile, concerning the place: from heaven, immediately to the synagogue, as it is said: 'to what we have come, this we do.' Marcion, take away also that from the Gospel: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and: 'it is not to take the bread of the sons and give it to dogs,' lest Christ seem to be of Israel. The deeds are enough for me instead of words. Take away the words of my Christ: the things will speak. Behold, he comes into the synagogue: certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold, he offers the bread of his doctrine first to the Israelites: certainly, as he prefers the sons. Behold, he does not yet impart it to others: certainly, as he passes over the dogs. To whom would he have imparted it more than to the strangers of the creator, if he himself were not first of the creator? And yet, how could he have been admitted into the synagogue so suddenly, so unknown, of whom no one was yet certain about the tribe, about the people, about the house, about the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives keep as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth? They certainly remembered, unless they knew he was circumcised, he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue was entered in a disorderly manner, nevertheless, one did not teach unless he was well-known and explored and proven long before, either in this or in some other commendation with this duty. They were all amazed at his doctrine. Certainly, because his word was in power, not because he was teaching against the law and the prophets. For divine eloquence, indeed, presents both the power and the grace, rather building up than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise, they would not have been amazed, but would have been horrified, and would not have marveled, but would have immediately turned away from the destroyer of the law and the prophets, and, indeed, in the first place, from the preacher of another god, because he could not have taught against the law and the prophets without a previously professed diversity and rivalry of divinity. When, therefore, the scripture does not signify anything of this kind, but only the power and authority of the word to amazement, it more easily shows that he taught according to the creator, because it does not deny it, than against the creator, because it does not signify it. And thus, either he is to be recognized as belonging to the one according to whom he taught, or he is to be judged as a transgressor, if he taught according to the one against whom he came. The spirit of the demon cries out there: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus? You have come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God.' I will not now retract, whether this title also suited him, whom it was not fitting to call Christ, if he was not of the creator - we have already demanded this elsewhere concerning the names - but now, as we dispute, how the demon recognized him by this title, with no preceding preaching having been sent out about him by the unknown god, and at that time, when he could not even have testified that he was holy, as unknown even to his own creator. What, therefore, had he already brought forth of such a new divinity, by which he could have been understood as the holy one of another god? Only that, having entered the synagogue and not having worked anything in his word against the creator? Just as, therefore, the one whom he did not know, he could not in any way have recognized as Jesus and the holy one of God, so the one whom he did know, he recognized. For he also remembered that the prophet had preached the holy one of God, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our Gospel: 'Therefore, because he will be born in you, he will be called holy, the son of God, and you will call his name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition - although he was a demon - rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he also said beforehand: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus?' not as if to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the creator pertain. For he did not say: 'What is there between you and us?' but 'What is there between us and you?' lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Which, seeing, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So much did he recognize Jesus as the son of the judge and avenger, and, as it were, of the severe God, not of the good one, who knows not how to destroy and punish. Why did we premise this passage? So that we may teach that Jesus was recognized by the demon, and not by another, and confirmed by himself, and not by another, as the one of the creator. 'But,' you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly, as one who was envious and impudent, even in his confession, as one who was flattering badly, as if this were the greatest glory of Christ, if he had come to the destruction of the demons, and not rather to the salvation of men, who did not want his disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If as one who had lied in everything, then Jesus was not the holy one of God at all; if as one who had lied in part, in that he considered him to be the holy one of God, indeed, but of the creator, he rebuked him most unjustly, for thinking what he knew was to be thought, and not estimating what he did not know was to be estimated: another holy one of the law, and of another god. But if the rebuke does not have a more probable status, unless we interpret it as we do, then the demon lied in nothing, nor was he rebuked for falsehood; for Jesus was the one whom the demon could not have recognized as another, and Jesus confirmed the one whom the demon recognized, while not rebuking the demon for falsehood.

pass_b_english: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius' reign, the story goes that Jesus descended into the city of Galilee, specifically Capharnaum, from the creator's heaven, which he had previously entered from his own heaven. But what's the logic behind this sequence of events? Why would Jesus first descend from his own heaven into the creator's heaven? It's worth questioning the narrative's consistency, especially since it often falls short of the truth. We've already discussed this elsewhere, so let's not repeat ourselves. The question remains: can Jesus be admitted by the creator and sent to earth if he's supposedly working against the creator? Now, I'm demanding a clearer explanation of Jesus' descent, assuming it happened. The fact that he appeared suddenly doesn't necessarily mean he descended - after all, a sudden appearance can be just that, a sudden sight. But if we're going to claim he descended, we need to know more about the circumstances: what he was wearing, what his attitude was, how he moved, and when exactly he descended. Who witnessed this descent, and who reported it? It's not like this is an easily believable story, even with someone vouching for it. It's surprising that Romulus had a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Jesus didn't have anyone to announce his descent from heaven - unless, of course, we're dealing with the same kind of fabricated story. So, what's the connection between Jesus and Galilee? If Galilee wasn't part of the creator's territory, why would Jesus go there to preach, especially when Isaiah says that this region is meant for the creator's people, who will see a great light and be freed from darkness (Isaiah 9:1-2)? If Marcion's god is the illuminator of the nations, wouldn't it make more sense for him to descend into Pontus rather than Galilee? Nevertheless, Jesus' actions in Galilee, particularly his teaching in the synagogue, suggest that he's fulfilling the creator's plan, not dissolving it. Marcion might try to erase this part of the story, but the facts speak for themselves. Jesus said he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them - and his actions prove it. Take away his words, and his deeds still testify to his mission. He went to the synagogue, where he taught the lost sheep of Israel, offering them the bread of his doctrine first, and only later to others. If he weren't part of the creator's plan, would he have prioritized the Israelites like this? And yet, how could he have been allowed into the synagogue, given that no one knew his tribe, people, or family, and he wasn't even registered in the Roman census? The archives keep a record of every birth, and they would have remembered if Jesus was circumcised - a requirement for entering the holy of holies. Even if the synagogue was open to anyone, teaching was only allowed for those who were well-known and respected. Everyone was amazed by Jesus' doctrine, but it was because his words were powerful and gracious, not because he was teaching against the law and the prophets. If he had been destroying the law, they would have been horrified, not amazed. The demon's cry in the synagogue - 'What do you have to do with us, Jesus? You've come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God' - is telling. The demon recognized Jesus as the son of the judge and avenger, the severe God, not the good one. But how did the demon know this, given that there was no prior preaching about Jesus from the unknown god? The demon must have known Jesus from the creator's realm, not from some new, alien divinity. After all, the prophet had already spoken of the holy one of God, and Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. The angel had also announced Jesus' birth, saying he would be called holy, the son of God. The demon's words - 'What do you have to do with us, Jesus?' - suggest a familiarity with the creator's spirits, not a stranger's. And when Jesus rebuked the demon, it was because the demon was being insincere, not because the demon was wrong about Jesus' identity. Jesus didn't want his disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the pure glory of salvation. So, why did he rebuke the demon? If the demon was lying, then Jesus wasn't the holy one of God; but if the demon was only partially wrong, assuming Jesus was the holy one of the creator, then Jesus' rebuke was unjustified. The fact that Jesus confirmed the demon's recognition of him, without rebuking the demon for falsehood, suggests that the demon was telling the truth - and that Jesus is indeed the holy one of the creator.

review.notes: Pass B fails on Scripture accuracy and completeness. 1. Scripture: Pass B cites (Isaiah 9:1-2) for the quote 'hoc primum bibito... lumen ortum est super uos', but the Latin text (and the actual biblical text alluded to) is Isaiah 9:1-2. While the citation is correct in content, Pass B's translation of the Latin 'regio Zabulon et terra Nepthalim...' is a paraphrase that omits the specific structure of the Latin text. More importantly, Pass B fails the completeness requirement by omitting several specific arguments and nuances present in the Latin and Pass A. 2. Completeness: Pass B omits the specific detail regarding the 'census of Augustus' being kept by 'Roman archives' (the Latin says 'domini natiuitatis Romana archiua', which Pass A translates as 'Roman archives keep as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth', but Pass B simplifies this significantly). 3. Completeness: Pass B omits the specific distinction in the final argument regarding the demon's rebuke: 'if as one who had lied in part, in that he considered him to be the holy one of God, indeed, but of the creator, he rebuked him most unjustly, for thinking what he knew was to be thought, and not estimating what he did not know was to be estimated: another holy one of the law, and of another god.' Pass B reduces this complex logical distinction to 'if the demon was only partially wrong, assuming Jesus was the holy one of the creator, then Jesus' rebuke was unjustified', losing the author's specific point about the demon's cognitive error regarding the 'other' god/law.
reasons: Pass B is a summary/paraphrase rather than a translation, failing the completeness requirement by omitting the specific logical nuances of the final argument ('thinking what he knew was to be thought...') and the specific details of the Roman archives/census argument.
